title: The edge-case habit, pulled together
idea: MEET (thinking), review-heavy. Consolidate the edge cases — empty, zero, one item, boundary, ties, all-fail — and the habit of listing them before coding.

exercises.prompt: What is an edge case, in one sentence?
options: An unusual input that can break a plan built for normal inputs
The first item in a list
exercises.explanation: An edge case is an unusual or extreme input — empty, zero, boundary — that ordinary-looking code can mishandle.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are edge cases worth listing when you plan? (Select all that apply.)
options: A value exactly on a cutoff
exercises.explanation: Empty, zero-divisor, boundary, and tie are all classic edge cases. Each stresses a plan in a different way.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: averaging an empty list is dangerous because...
options: count is 0 and dividing by 0 crashes
exercises.explanation: Empty means count 0, and total / 0 breaks. The empty guard protects the divide. A classic edge case.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: for 'passes if 50 or more', which input proves you used >= and not >?
exercises.explanation: The boundary value 50 is the test. With >= it passes; with > it would wrongly fail. Check the boundary directly.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: summing or counting an empty list is safely 0, but averaging it needs a guard.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Summing and counting nothing give 0 harmlessly. Averaging nothing divides by 0, so it needs a guard.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: match each problem to its signature edge case.
exercises.explanation: Averages fear empty; cutoffs fear the boundary; max fears empty and ties. Spotting these fast is the whole habit.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: put the edge-case-aware planning routine in order.
blocks: Understand the normal case and its answer
List the tricky inputs for this problem
Decide what each tricky input should do
Write code that handles the normal and tricky cases
exercises.explanation: Understand normal, list edge cases, decide each one's behavior, then code. Edge-case enumeration lives inside planning.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: a single-item list [7] is safe for totals and max, but risky for...
options: plans that compare each item to the NEXT one
exercises.explanation: One item has no 'next', so pair-comparing plans struggle. Totals, counts, and max handle a single item fine.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: if you filter then average, and no item passes, the danger is...
options: averaging over 0 matches — a divide by zero
exercises.explanation: An all-fail filter leaves 0 matches. Averaging them divides by zero — the same guard the empty case needs.

exercises.prompt: You've built the edge-case habit. The big takeaway:
options: Before coding, list the tricky inputs and plan for each — sturdier solutions, fewer surprises
exercises.explanation: Naming the empty, zero, one-item, boundary, tie, and all-fail cases up front makes your plans robust. A habit for every problem. Well done!
